newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed visits NATO military nerve centre. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed visits NATO military nerve centre. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: Russian security supremo Alexander Lebed arrived at the nerve centre of NATO's military machine on Tuesday as he continued his first trip to the West.
Lebed, an ex-paratroop general, is visiting NATO's military headquarters in southern Belgium for talks with General George Joulwan on Russia's participation in the Bosnian peace-keeping force.
Earlier on Tuesday he visited the headquarters of the Western European Union in Brussels as well as calling on Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet.
(Corrects name of organisation from Western European Alliance).

The gravel-voiced Lebed, a strong candidate to succeed President Boris Yeltsin if he has to bow out of office due to ill health, on Monday voiced grudging acceptance of NATO's plans to enlarge eastwards to take in some of Moscow's former satellites in eastern and central Europe.
"Whatever NATO decides, Russia is not going to go into hysterics," the 46-year-old Lebed told a news conference.
But Lebed left the door open to future discussion on NATO's relationship with Russia and the issue of expansion.

"We are all products, victims of the Cold War, we are not going to solve these problems in 24 hours," Lebed said after meeting with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and the ambassadors of the alliance's 16 member states.

Russia has tried to link enlargement with a new treaty or charter governing all relations between the two former Cold War foes. It sees expansion as a threat to its security. NATO rejects any idea of linkage.
Lebed said he accepted NATO's right to expand if it wished but said the problem was one of timing. "The main thing is not to hurry, or you may trip up," Lebed said.
NATO intends next year to invite countries to open entry talks with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic as the most likely candidates.
Some NATO diplomats interpreted Lebed's words as a signal that Moscow considered enlargement inevitable.
"He, above all, insisted on the question of timing as if the principle was now non-negotiable," said one ambassador.
